Q: (GNU) C23: How to define an constant array as a constant expression in C but keeping the defintion in a seperate C file? A:

The problem

However, as the array was declared static const the compiler placed it in the final binary several times.

Yes, this is to be expected. The identifiers of objects defined with internal linkage (from static) are local to the translation unit in which the definition appears, and those identifiers are available for any number of other internal-linkage objects (or functions) and up to one external-linkage object (or function). The so-defined objects and / or functions are all semantically distinct, with one of the implications being that they have distinct addresses. Under some circumstances, a compiler or linker might merge some of those as an optimization, but that cannot always be done, and you do not, in general, have any basis for expecting that.

In short: "the array" is a misconception. You defined multiple arrays. That may not have been what you intended to do, but it is not inherently erroneous.

the object definition was kept local to the translation unit. This allowed me to use that array in places where C expects a compile-time constant expression.

That there was a definition in each translation unit is also what gave you multiple arrays. Do not confuse definitions (a special case) with declarations (the general case).

In any event, it is true that having a definition in the translation unit contributed to being able to reference the array in initializers for objects with static storage duration (a different use of static), but you should understand that what is needed is a constant expression, which is a defined concept in C that doesn't necessarily align with your idea of a "compile-time constant".

Constant expressions are computable during translation (so probably during compilation, and certainly no later than during linking), but not all values that conceivably could be computed in that time frame satisfy the definition of a constant expression of the needed type. In your case, references to the arrays decayed to address constants, which can appear in integer constant expressions used in initializers.

I [...] changed the declaration in the header file to extern const and moved the actual definition into its own C file

And that is exactly the right thing to do to define one array instead of several. However, references to the array in other C files are then no longer address constants, so they cannot appear in initializers of objects with static storage duration. However, they can appear in initializers of objects with automatic storage duration.

It seems (that's how I understand it) that from the perspective of the C language constants which are not defined within the same translation unit are neither constant expressions nor compile-time constants. Am I correct here?

Not exactly. In the first place, the const qualifier does not make anything a constant. It is about whether modifications are permissible, not about whether they are possible. In the second place, the whole idea of translation units is that they bound a unit of information contributing to one translation effort, so definitions in a different translation unit are not directly relevant. It is only the [external] declarations in the same translation unit that make those other-TU objects accessible, and if you focus on each TU being compiled in isolation, it should be apparent why objects defined in one TU cannot appear in constant expressions in a different TU.

Solutions

What is the best solution for that kind of problem?

It depends. Among the possibilities are

Option 1: use automatic variables

For your particular example, a pretty good solution would be to use variables with automatic storage duration instead of static storage duration in your functions:

bar1.c

#include "pin_definitions.h"

void do_something_else( void ) {
    // not static; const optional:
    uint8_t const uint8_t shared_mode = pin_definitions[12].pin_mode
           || pin_definitions[89].pin_mode || pin_definitions[102].pin_mode;

    // ...
}

That variation does not require the initializer for shared_mode to be a constant expression. Semantically, the initializer is recomputed on each call, but

  • in most cases, that would be a sustainable cost, and
  • you can characterize it as a size vs speed tradeoff.

Option 2: use a compound literal

You could define a macro expanding to an array-literal version of your array, and use that instead. The caveat here is that you would be relying on your compiler to optimize away creation and storage of instances of the literal. You would want to verify that (remember to turn on optimization), else this could make your storage problem worse rather than better, but this is an optimization that I would expect many compilers to perform in the example given.

pin_definitions2.h

typedef struct __pin_definition_t {
    uint32_t pin_address;
    uint8_t pin_mode;
} pin_definition_t;

#define pin_definitions ((static const pin_definition_t[]) {  \
    { .pin_address = 0x0000000a, .pin_mode = 0xea },          \
    { .pin_address = 0x0000000f, .pin_mode = 0x12 },          \
    /* ... */                                                 \
})

#define pin_count ((uint_fast16_t) ((sizeof pin_definitions) / (sizeof (pin_definitions[0])))

Notes:

  • that derives the pin_count from the array, but you could also define it as a (lexical) constant if you preferred
  • Since C23, you can use constexpr instead of static const in the compound literal, if you prefer. That makes a slight semantic difference, and it is conceivable that your compiler would generate different code for that, but I doubt you would see a difference in practice.
  • C expressly provides that compound literals with const-qualified type, including those having constexpr storage duration, are not required to designate distinct objects. This opens the door to optimizing by merging these, but for the particular example shown, the optimization you're more likely to get is the whole object being optimized out, with the referenced member values alone being extracted.

Non-solutions

You asked about constexpr, but that doesn't do anything for you here by itself. A reference to an object defined in a different TU cannot appear in a constant expression, no matter the object's storage class. Conceptually, the object's value is not known in the context of compilation of a foreign TU.

Additional note

Again, const does not serve to declare constants. Among the implications is that with this definition:

static const uint_fast16_t pin_count = 345;

... references to identifier pin_count and expressions containing them are not integer constant expressions, even subject to the laxer rules governing initializers. As far as C is concerned, then, this:

static const pin_definition_t pin_definitions[pin_count] {
    // [...]

... is an attempt to declare a variable-length array with static storage duration (because it appears at file scope, not because of static), and that is not allowed. It is possible that your compiler accepts it anyway, as implementations are expressly permitted to accept forms of constant expression beyond those defined by the spec, but such a definition does not strictly conform. This one you can fix in C23 by changing const to constexpr.

Q: How to disable all hardware keys programmatically in Android? A:

Override onKeyDown and onKeyUp func, return them true, it means you handle press action yourself. In onKeyUp, you can implement more logic for each key press action if you want.
